title: Improving Sample Efficiency in Peptide-HLA Binding Prediction with Hybrid Quantum-Classical Neural Networks
authors: Chenyan Jia, Cong Guo, Siyue Chen, Pengpeng Ye, Xiaochun Chen
abstract: Peptide-HLA binding prediction is a critical step in neoantigen identification for personalized cancer immunotherapy and holds significant clinical value. However, the training data available for many HLA alleles are extremely limited, which severely constrains the performance of conventional methods on this task. Parameterized quantum circuits are hypothesized to induce inductive biases beneficial for learning from small datasets, yet their application to biological sequence prediction remains underexplored. To address this, we propose a hybrid quantum-classical neural network (HQNN) specifically designed for peptide-HLA binding prediction. HQNN integrates multi-source biological feature encoding with parallel quantum feature extractors and a quantum-enhanced classifier. On two HLA alleles (A*02:01 and B*07:02), HQNN outperforms a parameter-matched classical CNN baseline across all training sizes, with the performance gap widening as training data decreases. Ablation studies confirm the respective contributions of the quantum feature extraction module and the quantum classifier. In noise-aware simulations, performance degrades only mildly, and such degradation is reasonable and acceptable under realistic quantum hardware noise levels. These results suggest that hybrid quantum-classical architectures can provide practical sample-efficiency gains for immunoinformatics tasks in low-data regimes.
summary: This work proposes a Hybrid Quantum-Classical Neural Network (HQNN) to solve the data scarcity problem in predicting peptide-HLA binding for cancer immunotherapy. By integrating quantum feature extractors, the model demonstrates superior performance compared to classical methods, especially when training data is limited. This suggests that quantum machine learning architectures can provide practical, sample-efficient tools for complex biological prediction tasks.
main_problem: The core challenge is improving the sample efficiency of peptide-HLA binding prediction, which is crucial for personalized cancer immunotherapy but suffers from extremely limited training data for many HLA alleles.
main_result: The proposed Hybrid Quantum-Classical Neural Network (HQNN) consistently outperforms classical CNN baselines across all tested training sizes, with the performance gap widening significantly in low-data regimes.
method: The authors developed an HQNN that integrates multi-source biological feature encoding with parallel quantum feature extractors and a quantum-enhanced classifier.
model_or_system: The system models the binding interaction between peptides and HLA molecules. The model utilizes parameterized quantum circuits (PQC) within the feature extractor, processing encoded residue features to induce beneficial inductive biases for small datasets.
key_observables: AUC, AUPR, Accuracy, Precision, and Recall, measured across various training data proportions.
important_parameters: Low-data regimes (subsampling training sets down to 10% of original data); quantum hardware noise levels ($T_1, T_2$, gate error rates).
main_assumptions: The quantum circuits are assumed to provide practical sample-efficiency gains, and performance is tested under realistic, though simulated, quantum hardware noise levels.
figures_summary: Figures show dataset composition, performance comparison across training sizes (showing HQNN advantage), and t-SNE visualizations comparing feature clustering between HQNN and CNN embeddings.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the clinical need (neoantigen prediction), introduces the HQNN architecture (encoding, quantum feature extraction, classification), rigorously compares it against classical baselines (CNN, CAMP, NetMHCpan4.1), and validates its superior sample efficiency and robustness under noise.
why_interesting: The application of quantum circuits to encode complex, high-dimensional biological feature spaces (like amino acid properties) and enhance learning in data-scarce regimes is a direct intersection of quantum machine learning and biophysics, relevant to understanding complex system representations.
